implementation_notes: sync/atomic is the surface (Add, CompareAndSwap, Load, Store, Swap), and since Go 1.19 the typed wrappers - atomic.Int64, atomic.Pointer[T], atomic.Bool - remove the pointer-and-int32-cast ceremony that used to be required. Go's model is deliberately simpler than C++: all sync/atomic operations are sequentially consistent, there is no ordering parameter, and the Go memory model defines all atomic operations as if they behaved in some sequentially consistent order. That simplicity is why Go has no double-checked-locking bug: a channel send is a full synchronisation event, and the atomic operations carry the same guarantee. The tradeoff is that you cannot express a relaxed counter, so a hot counter pays more than it needs to.
idiom_name: sync/atomic typed wrappers (atomic.Int64, atomic.Pointer[T]) or package functions, all sequentially consistent
pitfalls: Go's atomics are all sequentially consistent - there is no relaxed counter, so a hot counter pays more than necessary; a mutex or per-CPU sharding can beat it.
64-bit values on 32-bit platforms are not atomic unless accessed through the typed atomic wrappers; a plain int64 field torn across a 32-bit word is a real bug there.
atomic.Pointer[T] is generic since 1.19; the older unsafe.Pointer-plus-uint32 idiom is error-prone and unnecessary on modern toolchains.
A spin loop with no Gosched starves the goroutine on a single-P runtime - Go's scheduler will not preempt a busy goroutine unless it reaches a blocking call.
